The pain and  reduced motion have markedly worsened over the past ___ years along with progressive stiffness that markedly impairs her activities of daily living as will be described further.  She says she first noticed herself limping six to ___ years ago, but the pain really had onset in the ___ of ___ after she  was diagnosed with malaria following a trip to ___.  Whether or not there is any relationship to contracting malaria and its possible sequelae and development of progressive rapid osteoarthritis and questionable underlying osteonecrosis is uncertain.  In any event, she is quite crippled by the arthritis and we see marked change in the radiographic appearance in the past ___ years of her hips and her ability to compensate for the stiffness, and the progressive pain is now more than she can continue to deal with.  She seeks total hip replacement.  Interestingly, she is a professor of anthropology, both at ___ and at ___ yet she commutes back and forth between ___ and ___ where her husband lives.  They have somewhat of a commuter marriage for the past quarter decade.  They are here together today.  At this point, she rates her pain in the hip as being worse on the right than the left, at rest ___, with activity 6 to ___  on VAS.  She has quite a bit of difficulty walking.  She uses a  cane all the time now, and surprisingly but with great difficulty remains able to get up and down four flights in her apartment in ___ daily.  She favors the right more than the left, finds it difficult to walk on uneven terrain.  ADLs are quite difficult, toileting is becoming a chore.  She has very little abduction and very little flexion through her hips.  Getting out of a chair requires maximal effort with push off, and when she attempts to sit down it is in a semi-recumbent position as she cannot flex the hips.  She has to teach standing up, which is painful.  She has a short shuffling gait as she cannot flex through her hips.  Her range of motion on the exam table is remarkable in that it has so little motion.  She is ___ feet 5 inches, 179 pounds, blood pressure 142/64, pulse 75.  Ambulating with a cane with a short shuffled gait.  As mentioned difficulty getting on to the table.  Hard to position herself in the chair.  She has only 30 degrees of flexion through either  hip and extends not to neutral.  There is virtually no internal and no external rotation through either hip, with perhaps 10 degrees of abduction with effort and woody crepitus and creaking from either hip joint. Clearly, she has wasting along the muscle groups of the hip.  Her knee motion is normal.  She has 1+ DP, ___.  In evaluating the consideration of whether or not malaria may have played some role in this rapid onset of arthritis, most likely it did not.  I have seen x-rays earlier from back in  ___, which was three months after her malaria and she had very severe arthritis in both hips with large osteophytes,  subchondral sclerosis, effacement of the joint and extensive osteophytes throughout.  In the two and a half years since, the appearance has worsened certainly.  There is complete absence now of definition of the articulation between the femoral head,  and  the acetabulum.  She is clearly going on to an auto fusion position.  When she contracted malaria back in ___, she was evaluated at the ___ infectious disease service, at which  time, she was noted to have extensive involvement.  Her smear showed greater than 15% parasite involvement of the erythrocytes.  This is plasmodium falciparum and she had to be immediately admitted to the ICU and it was felt that she was at severe disease risk because her high parasite load would put her at predisposition for capillary leakage, pulmonary edema, and respiratory  distress. She required a 14 unit exchange transfusion and treatment with quinidine and doxycycline.  She did have complications at that time with thrombocytopenia and acute renal failure, which resolved as did her acute transient confusion.  However, by ___, she was back to teaching but was having a lot more trouble walking and using the cane, favoring the right side,  etc.  Past Medical History:  Malaria ___, low back pain, osteoarthritis both hips with ankylosis, hard of hearing, reactive airway disease exacerbated by cats and dogs, colon adenoma. Assessment and Plan:  Professor ___ has severe bilateral hip osteoarthritis with a near ankylosis of both hips.  She is developing impending autofusion of the hips.  Whether or not there are some underlying contribution from her malaria causing avascular necrosis or more rapid progression of arthritis is indeterminate, but she has had severe arthritis on radiograph  for at least three or ___ years.  At this point, she has difficulty with ambulation, activities of daily living, toileting, chairs, stairs, etc.  She needs to use a cane all the time.  We have talked about her needs.  We are going to move forward with a staged bilateral total hip replacement.  She would need to avoid a same admission, bilateral total hip replacement as it would probably be excessive surgeries for her and she may have increased risk potentially given her history of malaria.  It is not clear again whether or not the malaria contributed in  anyway, but the amount of ankylosis and progressive arthritis is  markedly developed in the past ___ years.  As such, this will be a complex primary right total hip replacement, predominantly from the perspective of gaining access into the joint because of the extreme ankylosis;  quite likely she is going to need a full trochanteric osteotomy as opposed to a lateral osteotomy wafer.  As such, we will need to have ready the ___ claw and grip as well as a ___ cable.  We will likely need to take the capsule completely.  I anticipate as such, we may need to have ready constrained liners as resection of the labrum and capsule could set her up for long-term instability even though she has such limited range of motion now.  She does have muscle wasting, which will also contribute to potential for instability.  We  will have ready the ___ Secure Fit stems.  Whether or not she  will be able to donate blood, I have asked her to donate one or two units and will have a Cell Saver ready.  She realizes she does have increased risks for complications including infection, fracture, leg length discrepancy will be inevitable after one  hip is done and before the other is done.  Also at increased risk  for nerve palsy given the difficulty we are anticipating getting  into this hip.  It will be a strain on her.  Therefore, we will  likely favor the trochanteric osteotomy approach.  I think it is going to be longer for her to come back and for some patients, we anticipate having abductor precautions on her for some time.  If all goes well and she would have contralateral total hip replacement on the left a few months later.  She completes her academic teaching year on ___ and requests total hip replacement soon thereafter.  She signed the consent forms today in which I have gone over with her the increased risks across the board for complications given her presentation.   She understands this.  She has been given the THR information as well.  One final note is that she does not want to go to a subacute nursing facility as her mother apparently died of C. difficile in the past year at ___ and she finds that option very unnerving.
